The community garden started small — four raised beds behind the old firehouse — but its founders spent the winter mapping out something larger than a few rows of lettuce. They wanted a space where neighbors traded seedlings on Saturday mornings and shared the same rusted wheelbarrow without anyone keeping score of whose turn it was next.

By late spring the plot had grown past its original fence line — nobody had planned for that, least of all the volunteer who kept the sign-up sheet — and the extra rows went to tomatoes, squash, and a stubborn patch of mint that refused to stay in its bed. Visitors from the next block over started stopping by most evenings.

The soil there had never been tested before the project began — a fact that worried the retired chemistry teacher more than anyone else on the block — so the first month was spent hauling compost instead of planting anything at all. Patience turned out to be the hardest ingredient to source locally.

Water access was the next problem, since the nearest spigot sat two lots away — a detail nobody noticed until the first heat wave arrived — and hauling cans back and forth quickly became the least popular chore on the roster. A retired plumber eventually ran a line under the sidewalk for free.

Come August the beds were producing more than the neighborhood could eat on its own — an unusual complaint for a garden this young — so a folding table appeared at the corner every Thursday, stacked with whatever had ripened that week. Nobody kept a ledger of who took what.

The kids from the after-school program adopted one bed entirely for themselves — sunflowers, mostly, plus one doomed attempt at watermelon — and spent as much time arguing about watering schedules as they did actually watering anything. Their sunflowers still came in taller than the fence.

Winter forced a pause, though not the kind anyone expected — the ground froze hard enough to crack the older beds along one seam — and repairing the wood before spring became its own small neighborhood project, complete with borrowed drills and mismatched screws. The garden reopened a week ahead of schedule.

Looking back, the founders agree the garden never followed their original plan — every season rewrote the layout in some small way — and that turned out to be the part worth keeping, more than any yield count or ribbon from the county fair. The firehouse lot looks nothing like it did that first winter.
